content: The Ov-16 serology test should be used alongside the O-150 PCR test in black flies to confirm the interruption of Onchocerca volvulus transmission. This combined approach is necessary because relying on a single diagnostic method may not provide sufficient evidence for transmission interruption. The Ov-16 serology test should be conducted annually until the end of post-treatment surveillance, ensuring comprehensive monitoring of the elimination process. Challenges in implementation include difficulties in obtaining the minimum sample size of 2,000 children in endemic areas, which may limit the reliability of serological data. Research priorities include investigating the age-related and temporal dynamics of Ov-16 sero-reversion and validating the new Ov-16 Rapid Test as a potential replacement for the standard test. Skin snip microscopy, while historically used to monitor trends toward elimination, is no longer recommended for demonstrating the interruption of O. volvulus transmission in populations receiving mass drug administration (MDA). Its low sensitivity, estimated at 20%, and redundancy in the presence of O-150 PCR testing in black flies make it unsuitable for use at this stage of the program. However, during the transition to Ov-16 serology, skin snip microscopy may be used in parallel with serological testing to ensure programmatic goals are met with adequate statistical certainty. The Ov-16 serology test and skin snip microscopy were originally included in the 2001 WHO guidelines for certifying the elimination of human onchocerciasis. Since 2005, skin snip microscopy has been extensively used in APOC projects across Africa to monitor progress toward elimination. However, its declining sensitivity as programs approach the end of the treatment phase, coupled with high refusal rates in some communities, has led to its conditional recommendation against use. Despite its lower cost compared to O-150 PCR testing, the limitations of skin snip microscopy outweigh its benefits in low-prevalence settings. Ocular infection assessment, which involves identifying microfilariae in the anterior chamber of the eye, is also not recommended for confirming the interruption of O. volvulus transmission. This method requires specialized expertise and equipment, making it impractical and costly. Although it has been used in the past as a diagnostic tool, its undesirable consequences outweigh any potential benefits, particularly in the final stages of elimination programs. Post-treatment surveillance typically lasts 3–5 years and involves diagnostic tests such as O-150 PCR testing in black flies and, if necessary, Ov-16 serology testing in children under 10 years of age. These tests are conducted to confirm the interruption of transmission and the elimination of human onchocerciasis. The O-150 PCR test is particularly valuable for detecting the presence of infective stages of O. volvulus in black flies, providing critical evidence for assessing the risk of recrudescence. The Ov-16 serology test in children under 10 years of age is used under specific conditions, such as when PCR results are at or near the threshold for positivity. This ensures that any residual transmission is detected and addressed promptly. The conditionality of this recommendation reflects the need for careful interpretation of serological data in conjunction with entomological findings. The process of stopping MDA and transitioning to post-treatment surveillance involves several steps. A national oversight committee, independent of the national program, reviews program data to validate that transmission interruption criteria have been met. This committee advises the health ministry on whether to stop MDA based on entomological and serological test results. After a 3–5 year post-treatment surveillance period, the committee reviews all data to confirm the elimination of transmission and prepares a country report for submission to WHO. The international verification team, constituted by WHO, independently assesses the country report to verify the elimination of human onchocerciasis. This process ensures that the risk of reintroduction or recrudescence of infection is minimized, and that elimination criteria are met according to established guidelines.
